latin.599: At, inquiet aliquis, censemur apud Deum ac si iusti essemus. Nempe reuera iusti sumus, non iustitia legali sed evangelica, non iustitia operum sed fidei, non iustitia a nobis profecta aut acquisita, sed data a Deo & per fidem accepta. Dispar est ratio peccati: non promittitur, non datur a Deo, non accipitur a nondum existente.
latin.600: Verba Augustini causae meae non obsunt: fateor enim ab Adami vitio neminem esse immunem. Ad exemplum filiorum Saulis iam respondimus, eos paterni peccati fuisse participes. Peccata patrum visitantur in filiis, ut dixi, cum reperiuntur in filiis. Dicuntur patrum quia patres priores illa commiserunt, filiis ut committerent autores fuerunt, vel exemplo & autoritate, vel educatione & institutione, vel etiam lege.
latin.601: Objicies, quod etiam hoc loco subiungis Apostolum dixisse Levi fuisse decimatum in Abrahamo quia adhuc in lumbis patris erat, cum ei occurreret Melchisedec. Sed Apostolus satis innuit phrasim illam non modo non esse propriam, sed duram, cum eam emollivit hac praefatione ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν. Deinde ad locum illum respondi in thesibus, & tu meam responsionem tibi sumis refellendam in extremo cap. 9. tui tractatus; quam bene, cum tuis vestigiis insistens ad eum locum pervenero, Deo iuvante, ostendam, eademque opera ratiocinationem Apostoli retegam longe solidissimam, sed ab imputatione, quae inter nos controvertitur, alienam omnino.
latin.602: Objicis etiam similem phrasim in re simili eiusdem Apostoli: in Adam omnes moriuntur. Sed ea tuam sententiam evertit. Non vult enim omnes mori in Adamo illa ipsa singulari morte, qua mortuus est Adamus, quae scilicet omnibus imputetur, sed sua quisque propria morte. Sic vivificamur, seu resurgimus in Christo; non per imputationem resurrectionis Christi, sed reali, & quam quisque in se suscipit, resurrectione.
latin.603: Et cum versu praecedente Apostolus sic loquitur: quandoquidem per hominem est mors, etiam per hominem est resurrectio mortuorum, non intelligit unius Adami mortem reliquis hominibus imputatam nec unius Christi resurrectionem imputatam, sed mortem & resurrectionem specie unam, numero multam, qua omnes, quisque sua, moriuntur & resurgunt. Id ita manifestum est ut probatione non egeat.
latin.604: Concludamus igitur, cum idem Apostolus ait, per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introisse, intelligendum esse non singulare illud actuale peccatum quod unus ille homo commisit, sed peccatum ab illo natum, & in omnes homines sparsum ac propagatum: Et, cum ait, omnes peccasse in Adamo (quanquam id non dicit) intelligendum esse omnes peccasse, non uno illo singulari peccato actuali Adami illis imputato, sed suo quemque, sibi infito ac proprio peccato, quod ab illo Adami ducit originem. Morimur ergo in Adamo; id est, vi communionis naturalis quae nobis cum Adamo intercedit, non autem in ipsa Adami persona; & vivificamur in Christo, non in ipsa persona Iesu Christi, sed vi communionis nostrae supernaturalis cum ea: sed hac de re rursus cum ad Theses ventum fuerit.

pass_a.599: Placeus answers the 'reckoned as if just' comeback: we really are just—evangelical faith-righteousness given by God, not legal works-righteousness from us. Sin does not work that way: it is not promised, given by God, or received by someone not yet existing.
pass_a.600: Augustine's 'no one immune from Adam's vice' does not refute him—he grants it. Saul's sons already answered as sharers in the father's sin. Fathers' sins are visited when found in the sons; they are called the fathers' because fathers first did them and led sons into them by example, authority, upbringing, or law.
pass_a.601: Against the Heb. 7 Levi-in-Abraham proof: Paul himself marks the phrase as harsh and not proper ('so to speak'). Placeus says he already answered the place in the theses; Garrigues takes that answer to refute at the end of his ch. 9. Placeus will follow those steps later and show Paul's reasoning most solid—yet altogether foreign to the antecedent imputation under dispute.
pass_a.602: Against 1 Cor. 15 'in Adam all die': Placeus says the verse overturns the other side. Paul does not mean all die by Adam's one singular death imputed to everyone, but each by his own proper death. Rising in Christ matches that—real resurrection each receives in himself, not imputation of Christ's rising.
pass_a.603: On the prior verse (death and resurrection come by a man): not Adam's one death or Christ's one rising imputed to the rest, but death and rising one in kind and many in number, each his own. Placeus treats that as plain without further proof.
pass_a.604: Tip conclusion on Rom 5: when Paul says sin entered through one man, Placeus hears sin born from Adam and spread into all—not the singular paradise act imputed. The slogan 'all sinned in Adam' (which Paul does not say) means each by his own inborn proper sin from that origin. Dying in Adam is by natural communion with him, not by being in Adam's person; living in Christ is by supernatural communion—not by being in Christ's person. More when the Theses come. Natural tip before GAR Resp. 1.

599: But someone will say: we are reckoned before God as if we were just. Yes—we truly are just, not by a legal righteousness but by an evangelical one; not by a righteousness of works but of faith; not by a righteousness that proceeds from us or is acquired by us, but given by God and received through faith. The case of sin is different: it is not promised, not given by God, not received by one who does not yet exist.
600: Augustine's words do not hurt my case: for I grant that no one is immune from Adam's vice. As for the example of Saul's sons, we have already answered that they were partakers of the father's sin. The fathers' sins are visited on the sons, as I said, when they are found in the sons. They are called the fathers' because the fathers first committed them, and were authors to the sons that they should commit them—by example and authority, or by education and training, or even by law.
601: You will object that here too you add the Apostle's saying that Levi was tithed in Abraham because he was still in his father's loins when Melchizedek met him. But the Apostle plainly hints that that phrase is not only not proper, but harsh, when he softens it with the preface "so to speak." Next, I answered that place in the theses, and you take my answer to refute it at the end of chapter 9 of your treatise; how well, when following your steps I reach that place, God helping, I will show—and by the same work I will uncover the Apostle's reasoning as most solid, yet altogether foreign to the imputation disputed between us.
602: You also object a like phrase in a like matter from the same Apostle: in Adam all die. But that overturns your view. For he does not mean that all die in Adam by that very singular death by which Adam died, as if it were imputed to all, but each by his own proper death. So we are made alive, or rise, in Christ—not by imputation of Christ's resurrection, but by a real resurrection which each receives in himself.
603: And when in the preceding verse the Apostle speaks thus—since by a man comes death, by a man also comes the resurrection of the dead—he does not mean one Adam's death imputed to the rest of men, nor one Christ's resurrection imputed, but death and resurrection one in kind, many in number, by which all die and rise, each his own. That is so plain it needs no proof.
604: Let us conclude, then: when the same Apostle says that through one man sin entered the world, it is to be understood not as that singular actual sin which that one man committed, but as the sin born from him and spread and propagated into all men. And when it is said that all sinned in Adam (though he does not say that), it is to be understood that all sinned—not by that one singular actual sin of Adam imputed to them, but each by his own inborn and proper sin, which takes its origin from that of Adam. We die, then, in Adam—that is, by the force of the natural communion that joins us to Adam, not in Adam's own person; and we are made alive in Christ, not in the very person of Jesus Christ, but by the force of our supernatural communion with him: but of this again when we come to the Theses.
